{{Orphan|date=October 2022}}

'''Multiresolution Fourier Transform''' is an integral [[fourier transform]] that represents a specific [[wavelet]]-like transform with a fully scalable modulated window, but not all possible translations.<ref name="Grigoryan">{{cite book |last1=Grigoryan |first1=A. M. |title=Proceedings. (ICASSP '05). IEEE International Conference on Acoustics, Speech, and Signal Processing, 2005 |chapter=Multiresolution of the Fourier Transform |date=2005 |volume=4 |pages=577–580 |doi=10.1109/ICASSP.2005.1416074|isbn=0-7803-8874-7 |s2cid=18711567 }}</ref>

==Comparison of Fourier transform and wavelet transform==
The [[Fourier transform]] is one of the most common approaches when it comes to [[digital signal processing]] and [[signal analysis]]. It represents a signal through [[sine and cosine]] functions thus{{explain|date=July 2022}} transforming the [[time]]-domain into [[frequency]]-domain. A disadvantage of the Fourier transform is that both sine and cosine function are defined in the whole time plane, meaning that there is no time resolution. Certain variants of Fourier transform, such as [[Short-time Fourier transform|Short Time Fourier Transform]] (STFT) utilize a window for sampling, but the window length is fixed meaning that the results will be satisfactory only for either low or high frequency components. [[Fast Fourier transform|Fast fourier transform]] (FFT) is used often because of its computational speed, but shows better results for stationary signals.<ref name = "Grigoryan"/>

On the other hand, the [[wavelet transform]] can improve all the aforementioned downsides. It preserves both time and frequency information and it uses a window of variable length, meaning that both low and high frequency components will be derived with higher accuracy than the Fourier transform{{Citation needed|date=July 2022}}. The wavelet transform also shows better results in transient states{{Citation needed|date=July 2022}}. Multiresolution Fourier Transform leverages the advantageous properties of the wavelet transform and uses them for Fourier transform.<ref name = "Grigoryan"/>

==Definition==

Let <math>f(t)</math> be a function that has its Fourier transform defined as

: <math>F(\omega)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(t) \cos (\omega t) d t-j \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(t) \sin (\omega t) d t</math> &emsp;&emsp;{{EquationRef|(Eq.1)}}

The time line can be split by intervals of length π/ω with centers at integer multiples of π/ω

: <math>I_{n}=I_{n}(\omega)=\left[\frac{(2 n-1) \pi}{2 \omega}, \frac{(2 n+1) \pi}{2 \omega}\right), n=0, \pm 1, \pm 2, \ldots</math> &emsp;&emsp;{{EquationRef|(Eq.2)}}

Then, new transforms of function <math>f(t)</math> can be introduced

: <math>F_{\Psi}\left(\omega, b_{n}\right)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(t) \Psi_{\omega, b_{n}} d t</math> &emsp;&emsp;{{EquationRef|(Eq.3)}}
: <math>F_{\Psi}(0,0)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(t) d t</math> &emsp;&emsp;{{EquationRef|(Eq.4)}}

and

: <math>F_{\varphi}\left(\omega, b_{n}\right)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(t) \varphi_{\omega, b_{n}} d t</math> &emsp;&emsp;{{EquationRef|(Eq.5)}}
: <math>F_{\varphi}(0,0)=0</math> &emsp;&emsp;{{EquationRef|(Eq.6)}}

where  <math>b_{n}=b_{n}(\omega)=\frac{\pi}{\omega} n</math>, when n is an integer.

Functions <math>F_{\Psi}</math> and <math>F_{\varphi}</math> can be used in order to define the complex Fourier transform

: <math>F(\omega)=\sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty}(-1)^{n} F_{\Psi}\left(\omega, b_{n}\right)-\sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty}(-1)^{n} F_{\varphi}\left(\omega, b_{n}\right)</math> &emsp;&emsp;{{EquationRef|(Eq.7)}}

Then, set of points in the frequency-time plane is defined for the computation of the introduced transforms

: <math>B=\left\{\left(\omega, b_{n}\right) ; \omega \in(-\infty, \infty), b_{n}=n \frac{\pi}{\omega}, n=0, \pm 1, \pm 2, \ldots, \pm \mathrm{N}(\omega)\right\}</math> &emsp;&emsp;{{EquationRef|(Eq.8)}}

where <math>N(0)=0</math>, and <math>N(\omega)</math> is the infinite in general, or a finite number if the function <math>f(t)</math> has a finite support. The defined representation of <math>f(t)</math> with the functions <math>F_{\Psi}</math> and <math>F_{\varphi}</math> is called the B-wavelet transform, and is used to define the integral Fourier transform.

The cosine and sine B-wavelet transforms are:

: <math>f(t) \rightarrow\left\{F_{\psi}\left(\omega, b_{n}\right),\left(\omega, b_{n}\right) \in B\right\}</math> &emsp;&emsp;{{EquationRef|(Eq.9)}}
: <math>f(t) \rightarrow\left\{F_{\varphi}\left(\omega, b_{n}\right),\left(\omega, b_{n}\right) \in B\right\}</math> &emsp;&emsp;{{EquationRef|(Eq.10)}}

B-wavelet doesn't need to be calculated across the whole range of frequency-time points, but only in the points of set B. The integral Fourier transform can then be defined from B-wavelet transform using.<ref name = "Grigoryan"/>

Now Fourier transform can be represented via two integral wavelet transforms sampled by only translation parameter:

: <math>T_{\Psi}(\omega, \mathrm{b})=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(t) \Psi_{\omega, \mathrm{b}} d t</math> &emsp;&emsp;{{EquationRef|(Eq.11)}}
: <math>T_{\varphi}(\omega, \mathrm{b})=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(t) \varphi_{\omega, \mathrm{b}} d t</math> &emsp;&emsp;{{EquationRef|(Eq.12)}}

==Applications==
Multiresolution Fourier Transform is applied in fields such as image and audio signal analysis,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Wilson |first1=R. |title=A generalized wavelet transform for Fourier analysis: the multiresolution Fourier transform and its application to image and audio signal analysis |journal=IEEE Transactions on Information Theory |date=March 1992 |volume=38 |issue=2 |pages=674–690 |doi=10.1109/18.119730}}</ref> curve and corner extraction,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Davies |first1=A. R. |title=Curve and corner extraction using the multiresolution Fourier transform |journal=International Conference on Image Processing and Its Applications |date=1992 |pages=282–285}}</ref> and edge detection.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Li |first1=Chang-Tsun |title=1999 IEEE Workshop on Signal Processing Systems. SiPS 99. Design and Implementation (Cat. No.99TH8461) |chapter=Edge detection based on the multiresolution Fourier transform |date=1999 |pages=686–693 |doi=10.1109/SIPS.1999.822376|isbn=0-7803-5650-0 |s2cid=120165573 }}</ref>
